The city kept its lost things beneath the railway station.

Not just umbrellas and gloves. Those were upstairs, in plastic bins beside a man who ate oranges with a pocketknife.

The other things were downstairs.

You reached them by asking for a ticket to somewhere that no longer existed. The clerk would look at you for a moment, then slide a brass token under the glass.

Mara asked for a ticket to the house where she grew up.

“Single or return?” the clerk said.

She hadn’t expected that.

“Return.”

He gave her the token.

Below the station, the air smelled of dust and warm electrical wiring. A woman sat behind a desk, repairing a radio. Her gray hair was held back with two pencils.

“What have you lost?”

“My father’s voice.”

The woman set down her screwdriver.

“When?”

“Not when he died. Before that, I think. I can remember things he said, but when I try to hear him saying them, it’s my own voice.”

“People often come for that.” She pulled a drawer open. “Name?”

“His or mine?”

“His. Unless he was someone different with you.”

Mara gave both names.

The woman wrote them on a card and handed it to her.

“Aisle nine. You may hear things calling from other shelves. Don’t answer unless you’re certain they belong to you.”

Beyond the desk stood rows of shelves that disappeared into a darkness deeper than the room should have allowed. Each aisle had a hanging lamp. Under the lamps were boxes, bottles, envelopes, small wooden cabinets.

A jar labeled THE ABILITY TO SLEEP IN A MOVING CAR sat beside a shoebox marked CONFIDENCE, AGE ELEVEN.

Mara paused at an empty stretch of shelf.

“That’s for passwords,” the woman called. “They don’t stay long.”

In aisle four, something laughed behind a cabinet door. It was a boy’s laugh, breathless and delighted. She thought of a classmate whose name she had forgotten. She kept walking.

On a shelf in aisle seven lay a pair of blue mittens.

Her mother had knitted mittens just like them. Mara had lost one on a school trip, and her mother had made a third, slightly larger. For a winter she’d worn the mismatched pair. These were the same size.

She left them alone.

Aisle nine smelled faintly of coffee.

There were hundreds of voices. Some lived in seashells. Others were wound onto reels of tape or folded into paper birds. One came from a chipped cup: a woman saying, “Careful, it’s hot,” over and over.

Mara checked the names on the labels.

She found her father near the floor, between a tin of a grandfather’s whistling and an answering-machine cassette labeled DON’T WAIT UP.

His voice was in a plain brown envelope.

She crouched and held it.

Inside, he said, “Well, let’s have a look.”

She sat down on the floor.

He used to say that when she brought him broken things: a bicycle light, a school project, the little music box with a dancer who had stopped turning. Once, when she was seventeen, she’d brought him a letter she was afraid to send.

“Well, let’s have a look.”

The envelope was light enough to blow away.

She opened it.

“Hold this a second.”

“Where’s your mother?”

“No, the other screwdriver.”

“Oh, Mara.”

That last one hurt. She couldn’t place it. It might have been after she crashed the car, or when she arrived for a visit without warning. She tried to make him say it again, but now he was complaining about the price of pears.

She stayed on the floor until the lamp above her flickered.

Back at the desk, the woman had coaxed a weather forecast out of the radio. Rain was expected somewhere.

“Can I take it home?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“How do I keep it?”

“Listen occasionally. Don’t try to learn every word. And keep it away from magnets.”

“Might I lose it again?”

“You might.”

Mara looked down at the envelope. “What do I owe you?”

“Something you’re finished with.”

From beneath the desk, the woman brought out a shallow wooden tray.

“Not something you want to be finished with,” she added. “People offer grief all the time. It usually follows them out.”

Mara considered the small injuries she still carried. A friend who hadn’t called. Something cruel she’d said and never apologized for. The woman waited, working a thumb against a smear of solder on the desk.

Then Mara remembered a telephone number.

For years after leaving home, she could still dial it without thinking. It had belonged to the kitchen wall, to her mother shouting that dinner was ready, to her father taking messages on the backs of envelopes. The number had been disconnected long ago.

She spoke it into the tray.

Seven little clicks sounded against the wood.

The woman covered the tray with a cloth.

At the top of the stairs, Mara tried to remember the number. She knew the first digit had been a four, but couldn’t be sure of the rest.

Outside, rain darkened the pavement. She tucked the envelope inside her coat and hurried to the bus stop.

At home, she put the kettle on. Then she took the envelope out and set it on the kitchen table.

For a while it was quiet.

She found a mug, opened the cupboard, and discovered she was out of tea.

“Well,” her father said, “let’s have a look.”

Mara pulled up a chair.
